When Exile Becomes a Family Story

In this fragment of *Ecos del Exilio*, the interviewee describes how the experience of exile becomes a family anecdote repeatedly told to those who arrive later. The departure acquires a continuing role in family life: recounting it introduces new listeners to the past through which the family understands its origins (Bonilla). What began as an experience of displacement becomes a reference point for belonging.

Jan Assmann’s concept of communicative memory helps explain this practice. Memories are sustained through everyday conversation and relationships among people who share and interpret accounts of the past (126–27). In this reading, telling the story of exile offers newcomers a place within a family history that began before their participation in it. Belonging can develop through a relationship to experiences they did not personally live.

Robyn Fivush’s research on family reminiscing adds that storytelling communicates interpretations of why events matter. Through exchanges between narrators and listeners, memories acquire meanings that help people understand themselves in relation to others (46). The anecdote can therefore convey an explanation of how the family came to be where it is and why that departure remains significant. Its meaning may also develop as later listeners contribute questions and perspectives of their own.

This reflection helps us read the family histories narrated earlier by Gloria and Ana María. In their accounts, events experienced by one generation enter the explanations offered by another. By bringing these voices together, the documentary makes family storytelling visible as one of the practices through which memories of Cuban exile circulate in Puerto Rico. It also carries those accounts beyond the family, making their transmission itself a subject of public reflection.

Leaving Cuba: Economic Reconstruction and Family Separation

Leaving Cuba meant finding a way to sustain a family under new circumstances. In this segment, the documentary brings together the economic demands of establishing a household in Puerto Rico and the separation from relatives who remained on the island. For some professionals and members of the middle and upper-middle classes, departure disrupted an established livelihood and made previously familiar forms of security uncertain.

Jorge Duany’s research helps situate these experiences within the history of Cuban settlement in Puerto Rico. He describes an initial decline in occupational status among many exiles, alongside the resources that facilitated economic recovery. Some migrants brought capital or professional skills; others obtained credit through earlier banking relationships or formed businesses with relatives and friends. Accounts of beginning again must therefore be understood in relation to these unequal resources: losing property or employment could coexist with retaining knowledge and connections that helped support a household after departure (95).

Rebuilding a household in Puerto Rico also raised questions about how to maintain relationships with relatives in Cuba. Opportunities to visit depended partly on government authorization. In its original wording, Article 1 of Cuba’s 1976 Migration Law required citizens holding ordinary passports to obtain permission from the Ministry of the Interior to enter or leave the country (Cuba, art. 1). U.S. regulations governing travel-related transactions imposed additional constraints. In 2004, authorized visits to immediate family were limited to once every three years, for no more than fourteen days, and required a specific license (Office of Foreign Assets Control 33769). In September 2009, the U.S. Department of the Treasury removed those frequency and duration limits (“Fact Sheet”). These changes made the possibilities of reunion dependent on shifting permissions and definitions of eligible family relationships.

Within Cuba, institutional restrictions and political pressures could also discourage communication. María de los Ángeles Torres documents prohibitions on correspondence for party militants and identifies writing to relatives abroad as a criterion used to deny university admission (51). Velia Cecilia Bobes likewise notes that, from the 1960s through the late 1980s, correspondence with relatives or friends abroad could obstruct admission to the Communist Party or the Union of Young Communists, as well as access to certain public positions (note 13). These practices operated differently from restrictions on travel: they made maintaining a family relationship potentially consequential for the educational or professional opportunities of those who remained.

Read within this context, the segment places the departing family within a wider history of economic reconstruction and interrupted relationships. Establishing a livelihood in Puerto Rico could gradually become possible while ordinary forms of family life—visiting, sharing responsibilities, and being present for one another—remained difficult to sustain. The household that emigrated continued to belong to relationships extending beyond its new home, under conditions shaped by both material resources and political decisions.

Nostalgia, Uprootedness, and Psychological Adjustment

The psychological impact discussed in this segment concerns the difficulty of continuing with everyday life after separation from familiar people and places. The demands of settling elsewhere could arrive before a person had time to absorb what departure meant. Dinesh Bhugra and Matthew Becker examine these experiences through cultural bereavement: the grief that can accompany disruption to familiar practices, social networks, and established understandings of oneself. Their approach draws attention to how economic uncertainty and reduced social support can intensify the emotional demands of migration (18–19, 23).

The concept of place attachment helps explain why these feelings can remain closely connected to particular homes, neighborhoods, and landscapes. Leila Scannell and Robert Gifford describe how places become meaningful through personal memories and shared experiences (2–3). Read through this framework, the nostalgia voiced in the documentary expresses an attachment to the relationships and routines through which Cuba became home. Remembering a place can also mean remembering who one was there: a relative surrounded by family, a professional whose work was recognized, or someone whose daily life unfolded among familiar people.

These attachments help explain why emotional adjustment may follow a different course from economic recovery. A person can establish a household and regain financial security while continuing to feel the absence of relatives and an earlier way of life. Bhugra and Becker emphasize the importance of social support and the circumstances of settlement in shaping how such losses are experienced (19, 23). Applied to this fragment, their work suggests that nostalgia forms part of the ongoing effort to live with separation. New relationships and routines can gradually make life in Puerto Rico familiar, while memories of Cuba continue to give meaning to the life that preceded departure.

“The Other Cuba”: Prosperity, Inequality, and Political Memory

The Cuba remembered in this segment belonged to a period of considerable commercial and cultural vitality. For some members of the early exile community, the 1950s remained associated with professional opportunities, family security, and participation in a society connected to international markets and cultural life. Understanding these recollections requires attention to the achievements that made such experiences possible, alongside the conditions that limited access to them.

Tourism provides one measure of Cuba’s international prominence. In 1957, the island received 272,266 international tourists, compared with 187,321 in Puerto Rico. By 1958, Cuba had 7,728 hotel rooms, with approximately 72 percent concentrated in Havana and Varadero (Perelló Cabrera 2). Hotels, casinos, restaurants, and entertainment venues formed part of an expanding infrastructure that connected the island to international visitors and investment. Their visibility helped establish an enduring image of Havana as a sophisticated Caribbean capital.

Commercial life extended beyond the tourist industry. Marifeli Pérez-Stable documents a consumer boom during which Cuba imported an annual average of 30 million pesos in automobiles and 45 million pesos in household durable goods. Installment purchasing became increasingly familiar, while department stores in New York and California advertised in Havana newspapers (31). Shops, advertising, imported merchandise, and access to consumer credit formed part of the urban experience. Cultural production also circulated internationally: Cuban musicians toured throughout the Americas and Europe, while foreign performers appeared on Cuban stages (Moore 42–43). For those who participated in this world, memories of modernity and abundance had concrete foundations.

These developments coexisted with substantial differences in living conditions. The 1953 census recorded the following contrasts:

| Indicator, 1953 | Urban areas | Rural areas |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Illiteracy among people aged ten and older | 11.6% | 41.7% |
| Homes with electricity | 82.9% | 8.7% |
| Homes with running water inside the dwelling | 57.7% | 6.7% |

Sources: Pérez-Stable (28), for illiteracy; International Commission of Jurists (24–25), for housing services.

The figures show how commercial sophistication and uneven development could exist within the same national economy. Access to electricity, education, and domestic amenities differed sharply according to place of residence. Within cities, class and racial inequalities further shaped opportunities for employment, housing, and recreation (Moore 31). Speaking of “two Cubas” can help students recognize these contrasting experiences, provided the phrase remains attentive to the differences within urban and rural society.

Economic and cultural achievements also developed under increasingly repressive political conditions. Batista’s military coup in March 1952 interrupted constitutional government, and violence against political opponents intensified during the final years of his rule (Moore 29–30). Parts of the casino industry operated through profitable relationships between organized crime and the regime, connecting commercial expansion to political patronage and corruption (33–34). The prosperity visible in hotels, shops, and entertainment venues consequently belonged to a society in which political participation and personal safety could be severely constrained.

After 1959, agrarian reform, urban housing reform, and nationalization transformed the economic relationships through which many families had organized their lives. Duany identifies these policies among the changes that adversely affected sectors of the middle and upper classes during the early revolutionary years (76). For some exiles, the loss of property, professional standing, or economic security became central to the meaning of the Revolution. Their remembered Cuba preserved a world in which they had worked, formed relationships, and imagined a future.

Jan Assmann’s account of collective memory helps explain how these experiences can become shared interpretations of the past. Memory reconstructs earlier life through the concerns and social frameworks of the present (130). In this fragment, nostalgia can be read as an attachment to a historically real world whose opportunities were unevenly distributed. Remembering that world with affection does not establish support for Batista; nor does acknowledging its achievements resolve the question of who benefited from them. A fuller reading holds together Cuba’s economic and cultural accomplishments, its social inequalities, and the repression that shaped political life, then asks how different experiences of that society informed the memories carried into exile.

Blame, Political Promises, and the Decision to Leave

The reproaches discussed in this segment turn Cuba’s political history into a question of personal responsibility. One accusation holds those who supported Fidel Castro and the July 26 Movement responsible for helping bring the revolutionary government to power. Another faults those who emigrated for leaving others to confront its consequences. Both interpret individual decisions through the subsequent history of the country, raising questions about what people expected, what they could know, and how much influence they could exercise over political change.

The public commitments associated with the July 26 Movement provide an essential starting point. The Sierra Maestra Manifesto, signed by Fidel Castro, Felipe Pazos, and Raúl Chibás on July 12, 1957, proposed a provisional government followed by general elections within a year under the Constitution of 1940. It promised freedom of the press, constitutional protections, the release of political prisoners, and free trade-union elections. Its social program included a campaign against illiteracy, industrial development, job creation, and agrarian reform with compensation for previous landowners (Castro et al., pts. 7–8). These commitments offered grounds for supporting the struggle against Batista while anticipating a constitutional government and substantial social reform.

The political system that subsequently emerged developed through decisions and conflicts after the revolutionary victory. Pérez-Stable describes the movement’s economic proposals as nationalist reformism, advocating a stronger role for the state alongside Cuban public and private investment (63). Castro publicly proclaimed the Revolution’s socialist character on April 16, 1961, when agrarian reform and extensive nationalizations had already transformed economic life (Castro, “Proclama”; Pérez-Stable 80–81). The declaration named a transformation already underway. This chronology matters when assessing earlier support: opposition to Batista and endorsement of the movement’s announced program did not necessarily entail agreement with the institutions and policies later established.

The accusation directed at those who emigrated introduces a related problem: the relationship between departure and political opposition. Drawing on Albert O. Hirschman’s concepts of exit and voice, Bert Hoffmann examines how emigration could relieve pressures on the Cuban government. His analysis also emphasizes the importance of state control over the conditions of departure and the emergence of political activity abroad (11–14, 26–27). Emigration could alter the possibilities of opposition within Cuba while creating other forms of political participation beyond its borders. Its consequences therefore require examination through government policies, institutional constraints, and the actions of migrants themselves.

Read through these approaches, the segment reveals a struggle over how responsibility is remembered and assigned between those who left and those who remained. The reproaches contain assumptions about alternative histories: that withdrawing support earlier, or remaining in Cuba, would have produced a different political outcome. Such possibilities can be investigated, but the accusation itself cannot establish them. For students, the challenge is to reconstruct the expectations and opportunities available at particular moments, while distinguishing the influence of ordinary citizens from the authority exercised by those who made and enforced government decisions.

Family Memory and the Possibility of Visiting Cuba

Ricardo Nieves, identified in the documentary as a member of the third generation and born in Puerto Rico, describes a relationship to Cuba shaped by respect and disagreement. He acknowledges his grandparents’ convictions and the pain associated with his parents’ experiences, while questioning why those histories should prevent him from visiting Cuba in the future. His reference to a special permit places official authorization alongside another consideration: his family’s acceptance of such a journey. The disagreement concerns the authority that the inherited past should exercise over his own decisions.

Robyn Fivush describes family remembering as a social process in which interpretations are shared, negotiated, and contested (46). This approach helps explain how Ricardo can recognize the significance of his relatives’ experiences while reaching a different conclusion about travel. His response shows family memory being actively interpreted. The history remains meaningful to him, even as he questions the expectations attached to it. Respect for the people who transmit a narrative can coexist with disagreement about what that narrative requires of subsequent generations.

Marianne Hirsch’s concept of postmemory offers a further way to examine this relationship. Developed in Holocaust studies, postmemory describes how descendants can become deeply connected to earlier generations’ traumatic experiences through stories, images, and behaviors encountered within family life (106–07). Applied cautiously here, the concept helps us distinguish Ricardo’s mediated relationship to the family past from the experiences of those who lived through it. The pain he acknowledges can carry considerable emotional weight without giving Cuba the same meaning for every family member. His account allows us to consider how an inherited history of loss may influence attitudes toward a country while leaving room for descendants to develop different relationships with it.

Puerto Rico is central to that possibility. Ricardo approaches Cuba from a different biographical position, formed outside the circumstances that shaped his relatives’ earlier decisions. Stuart Hall’s understanding of cultural identity as an ongoing historical process helps situate this difference: identities develop through changing experiences and positions, including the relationship between inherited histories and present circumstances (394–95). Ricardo’s position can therefore be understood through the interaction between his family’s Cuban past and his own life in Puerto Rico.

Within this reading, the possibility of visiting Cuba becomes a question about how to carry a family history forward. A journey could allow Ricardo to encounter the country through experiences of his own, while continuing to recognize the losses and convictions of his relatives. The fragment brings into view a difficult intergenerational negotiation: how to acknowledge another person’s pain while developing the freedom to decide what relationship that history will have to one’s own future.

Revolutionary Belonging, Family Support, and Political Judgment

Olga in this segment,  acknowledges that everyday survival has come to depend on assistance from relatives abroad. These observations concern different moments in her life: an earlier expansion of opportunity and a later experience of material insecurity. Their coexistence raises a question about how the political significance of an earlier benefit endures when the conditions of everyday life have changed.

Her account places family assistance within the changing relationship between households and the Cuban state. Susan Eckstein’s research describes how, following the loss of Soviet aid and trade, the government encouraged remittances as a source of foreign currency, while households sought resources unavailable through their existing incomes. These transfers supported recipients and generated resources for the state, even as they introduced tensions into the revolutionary economic and social order (Eckstein). Olga’s account brings this process into the documentary through the practical question of how people obtain what they need to live. Relatives abroad become participants in sustaining life on the island.

Olga attributes these difficulties to the U.S. embargo. Its effects require serious consideration: Amnesty International’s 2013 report noted UN agencies’ findings concerning its negative consequences for health and wellbeing. Establishing the relative contribution of sanctions, domestic policies, and other economic changes nevertheless requires evidence beyond an individual interview. Within Olga’s narrative, attributing hardship to external pressure allows criticism of present conditions to coexist with her recognition of what the Revolution made possible earlier in her life. This is one way of interpreting how she connects her biography to Cuba’s political history.

Her assertion that freedom of expression exists on the island requires a separate assessment. The Constitution then in force recognized speech and press freedoms according to the objectives of socialist society; Article 62 prohibited exercising recognized freedoms against the existence and purposes of the socialist state (Cuba, arts. 53, 62). Amnesty International’s 2013 report, covering events in 2012, documented restrictions on independent journalism and the detention of peaceful demonstrators and government critics. These conditions place limits on treating Olga’s statement as a description applicable to everyone.

Alessandro Portelli’s approach to oral narrative helps retain the significance of this discrepancy: recorded accounts provide evidence of the meanings people give to their experiences as well as information about events (52). Olga’s account therefore invites attention to how she understands freedom, evaluates responsibility for hardship, and connects political judgment to her own history. The fragment shows how recognition of material deprivation can coexist with continuing attachment to the Revolution.

Emigration, Exile, and the Conditions of Choice

For Andrés Candelario, the distinction between an emigrant and an exile concerns the circumstances that give departure its meaning. He contrasts leaving because one wishes to live elsewhere with leaving to secure the possibility of thinking and speaking freely. His account also includes economic pressures within the experience of exile and extends across different forms of departure. The central issue becomes what a person feels able to preserve—or compelled to relinquish—by remaining in Cuba.

Hein de Haas’s aspirations–capabilities framework offers a way to examine the relationship between choice and constraint. He understands human mobility through people’s practical freedom to choose where to live, including the possibility of staying. Migrants may exercise considerable initiative while confronting circumstances that severely restrict their alternatives; conversely, people who wish to leave may lack the resources to do so (de Haas). Applied to this fragment, the framework helps explain how an actively planned departure can nevertheless be experienced as necessary. The capacity to arrange a journey does not establish that remaining was a viable option.

Candelario’s inclusion of economic reasons also opens a conversation about how migration is classified. Jorge Duany identifies material deprivation and family reunification as increasingly prominent motivations during the Cuban migration of the 1990s, while tracing changes in the political and social composition of successive departures (84–85). Candelario approaches the distinction from another direction: economic pressures can belong within his understanding of exile. Read together, these perspectives encourage attention to how political institutions, opportunities to earn a livelihood, and restrictions on expression may shape the same decision to leave.

The terms emigrant and exile consequently need careful handling. Emigration describes movement away from a country of residence; exile can express the political circumstances and personal meaning attributed to that movement. The same person may understand their departure through both terms. Candelario’s formulation provides a broad language for recognizing experiences of constraint, although that interpretation should remain open to comparison with how other participants describe their own decisions.

Within the documentary, his distinction also connects departure to the possibility of living according to one’s convictions. The question extends beyond whether someone physically chose to leave: it concerns the alternatives available and the consequences of staying. His account places the freedom to speak, think, and sustain a livelihood within the discussion of what makes a place possible to remain in.

Berta Soler, the Damas de Blanco, and the Hope of Return

In this fragment, *Ecos del Exilio* presents a brief passage from a speech by Berta Soler in which she expresses the hope that political exiles and other Cubans living abroad will be able to return to the island. Her words introduce the possibility of a future reunion into the documentary’s accounts of departure and separation. Within this context, return can be understood as more than a journey: it raises questions about the conditions under which people might once again imagine a life in the country they left.

Soler is a cofounder of the Damas de Blanco, or Ladies in White, a peaceful protest movement that emerged in Cuba in 2003. Women organized following the imprisonment of 75 government critics, demanding the release of their husbands and other relatives. Their white clothing and Sunday processions after Mass became recognizable expressions of their campaign. By 2012, following the release of the prisoners whose incarceration had prompted its formation, the movement continued advocating for other political prisoners and broader civil and political freedoms (Amnesty International).

Trained in microbiology, Soler worked as a hospital technician in Havana before becoming a prominent opposition activist. Her husband, Ángel Moya Acosta, was among those imprisoned during the March 2003 crackdown known as the Black Spring. His imprisonment brought her into the collective organizing that gave rise to the Damas de Blanco. In 2011, following the death of cofounder Laura Pollán, Soler assumed the movement’s leadership (George W. Bush Presidential Center).

Read alongside this history, her appeal connects the hopes of Cubans abroad with struggles over political rights within Cuba. It also brings the documentary’s discussion of exile into a shared conversation about the island’s future. The possibility of return becomes a way of imagining a national community in which political disagreement need not sever a person’s relationship with their country. This reading leaves room for the different meanings that return may hold: visiting relatives, renewing relationships, or considering a more lasting presence on the island.

Cuban and Puerto Rican: Connected Histories of Belonging

In this fragment, participants turn to the historical connections between Cuba and Puerto Rico to explain their sense of belonging to both islands. References to independence struggles, José Martí, and poetry give their identifications a history that precedes the migrations discussed elsewhere in the documentary. Through these connections, they present feeling Cuban and Puerto Rican as compatible attachments, sustained by a shared past as well as by their own experiences.

The nineteenth-century struggle against Spanish colonial rule provides an important context for these references. Founded under José Martí’s leadership in 1892, the Partido Revolucionario Cubano sought Cuban independence while also committing itself to encouraging and assisting Puerto Rican independence. That commitment appears explicitly in the first article of its founding principles, the *Bases del Partido Revolucionario Cubano* (Martí, art. 1). The connection invoked in the documentary therefore had an organizational and political expression: the liberation of the two islands was articulated as an interconnected project.

The image of Cuba and Puerto Rico as the two wings of a bird comes from the Puerto Rican poet Lola Rodríguez de Tió. In “A Cuba,” she writes, “Cuba y Puerto Rico son / De un pájaro las dos alas”—Cuba and Puerto Rico are the two wings of a bird. The poem also describes a Puerto Rican speaker arriving in Cuba, mourning the home she has left while finding affection and the possibility of establishing another. Read alongside the documentary, this movement in the opposite direction is significant. It places the participants’ attachment to Puerto Rico within a longer history in which people have crossed between the islands and imagined belonging beyond their birthplace (Rodríguez de Tió).

Stuart Hall’s account of cultural identity helps explain how these attachments can coexist. Hall understands identity as a continuing process shaped by history and by the positions people occupy within changing circumstances (394–95). From this perspective, identification with Puerto Rico can become part of a person’s life without requiring the abandonment of Cuban belonging. The two affiliations may acquire different meanings through residence, relationships, memories, and participation in everyday life.

What makes the fragment especially revealing is the work that historical memory performs in the present. By recalling Martí and Rodríguez de Tió, the participants give their own sense of connection an older language of solidarity. Their account makes belonging to both islands intelligible through a history they recognize as shared. Feeling Cuban and Puerto Rican becomes a way of locating themselves within that history while describing the lives they have made.

Roots, Citizenship, and Different Ways of Belonging

Cuban roots acquire different meanings in this fragment of *Ecos del Exilio*. Some participants describe an enduring Cuban identification that accompanies them through life in Puerto Rico. Others explain how their sense of being Cuban or Puerto Rican becomes more prominent according to the occasion or the people around them. These accounts reveal differences within the diaspora, as well as changes in how individuals understand and express their own attachments.

Peggy Levitt and Nina Glick Schiller offer a useful distinction between “ways of being” and “ways of belonging.” The former concerns the relationships and practices in which people participate; the latter concerns actions through which they consciously express an identification. Living within a particular social environment does not automatically determine the identity a person claims. Equally, identification with a place can remain important through memory and imagination even when direct contact is limited (1010–11). Applied to this fragment, their distinction helps explain how participation in Puerto Rican life can coexist with a continuing sense of being Cuban.

The accounts of naturalization introduce another dimension. Puerto Rico falls within the geographical definition of the United States under U.S. immigration and nationality law; the naturalization discussed here concerns acquiring U.S. citizenship (8 U.S.C. sec. 1101(a)(38)). That legal membership must be distinguished from the participants’ Cuban and Puerto Rican identifications. For those who describe naturalization primarily as a legal procedure, the change in status does not define their understanding of who they are. For others, taking the oath carries considerable personal significance. The ceremony brings a public declaration of allegiance into contact with attachments formed through earlier experiences, relationships, and memories.

The differences surrounding the oath are therefore part of the fragment’s contribution. A procedure with a prescribed legal meaning can be experienced differently by the people who undertake it. Its emotional significance cannot simply be inferred from the acquisition of citizenship. The documentary places these interpretations alongside one another, showing how the relationship between legal membership and personal belonging is understood and narrated by particular individuals.

Levitt and Glick Schiller also emphasize that incorporation into a new society and continuing attachments elsewhere can develop simultaneously, changing in prominence across different circumstances (1011). This perspective accommodates movement between Cuban and Puerto Rican identifications while leaving room for those whose Cuban identification remains more constant. Read alongside the preceding discussion of historical connections between the islands, the fragment shifts attention from a shared language of solidarity to the varied lives through which that connection takes shape. Roots, residence, citizenship, and self-identification can overlap without carrying the same meaning for every member of the community.

Casa Cuba: Keeping Traditions Alive across Generations

At Casa Cuba, the effort to keep Cuban traditions alive brings together grandparents, children, and grandchildren. In this fragment, cultural practices become part of the relationship between generations: older participants seek to maintain familiar customs, while younger family members encounter those traditions within their lives in Puerto Rico. The institution provides a setting where connections to Cuba can be sustained through participation. Preserving the past becomes an activity undertaken in the present, involving people whose experiences of Cuba differ.

Jan Assmann’s distinction between communicative and cultural memory helps explain this process. Communicative memory develops through everyday exchanges between people, while cultural memory draws on more organized practices and forms of representation that sustain collective references to the past (126–28). Casa Cuba can be read as bringing these processes together. Contact between generations creates opportunities to exchange experiences, while institutional activities provide recurring occasions for customs identified as Cuban to be learned and practiced. The continuity of memory depends on people making those practices meaningful to others.

This work also gives nostalgia a social form. In the introduction to *The Future of Nostalgia*, Svetlana Boym connects longing for home with a desire for continuity and community amid displacement and historical change. Her account helps illuminate what may be at stake in maintaining traditions at Casa Cuba: familiar practices can recreate a sense of connection while offering something that participants hope younger generations will carry forward. Nostalgia can therefore influence how the community imagines its future as well as how it remembers Cuba.

For younger participants who did not experience their relatives’ departure from Cuba, the relationship to that past is mediated. Marianne Hirsch’s concept of postmemory, developed through Holocaust studies, examines how traumatic experiences can profoundly shape later generations through inherited stories, images, and behaviors (106–07). This concept becomes relevant when family accounts of exile and loss acquire that formative emotional force. Cultural transmission describes the broader process visible in the effort to preserve traditions; postmemory offers a more specific lens for examining inherited relationships to rupture and displacement.

The interviewee’s judgment that younger generations cannot be considered fully Cuban introduces a tension into this project of continuity. His assessment draws a boundary around cultural belonging even as the institution encourages traditions to pass between generations. A distinction emerges between transmitting Cuban practices and recognizing later generations as people entitled to interpret their own relationship to Cuba. Read alongside the preceding accounts of identity, his position represents one understanding of Cubanness within a varied community. Casa Cuba’s activities may sustain cultural connections precisely by allowing people with different experiences and affiliations to participate in them.

Remaining Cuban, Making a Home in Puerto Rico

Remaining Cuban and embracing Puerto Rico are presented in this fragment as connected parts of building a life after migration. The reflection also concerns the children: accepting the place where the family now lives may help them grow up with a sense of belonging, without expecting them to experience an earlier generation’s exile as their own. The speaker’s concern gives cultural identification an intergenerational dimension. It involves deciding what to preserve from the past and what possibilities to make available to those who come after.

Peggy Levitt and Nina Glick Schiller argue that incorporation into a new society and continuing attachments to a place of origin can develop simultaneously (1011). This perspective helps explain the position articulated here. Embracing Puerto Rican life can become part of how Cuban identification is lived after migration. The particular contribution of this fragment is to connect that possibility with a parental aspiration: children should have room to develop attachments grounded in their own experiences.

Family memory is central to that process. Robyn Fivush explains that remembering within families involves interpreting the significance of events, with meanings shared, negotiated, and reconsidered through interaction (46). Applied to this fragment, her account helps distinguish preserving knowledge of a family’s departure from making exile the defining condition of its descendants. Children can learn why their relatives left Cuba and understand the importance of that experience while developing their own relationship with Puerto Rico. The speaker’s reflection concerns the place that the history of displacement should occupy within their lives.

Read alongside the discussion of Casa Cuba, this position offers another understanding of cultural continuity. Keeping Cuban traditions alive and allowing children to feel at home in Puerto Rico can belong to the same family project. The emphasis falls on what the next generation should be able to build, as well as what it should remember. Accepting a new life becomes meaningful partly through this concern for the children’s future: Cuban heritage remains available as a source of connection, while their sense of home is given space to take shape.

Remembering 1950s Cuba: Exile and Selective Memory

In this fragment, nostalgia for 1950s Cuba becomes a framework through which a group of participants understands exile. The remembered country provides a point of reference for interpreting departure, loss, and the changes brought by the Revolution. Their relationship to Cuba is organized around a particular historical moment and the world they associate with it. Remembering that world helps give continuity to lives interrupted by migration.

Jan Assmann explains that cultural memory reconstructs the past through the frameworks and concerns of the present (130). Applied here, his argument helps us understand how experiences of loss can become organized into a shared narrative. Particular memories acquire significance beyond the individuals who recount them: they help establish what the group understands itself to have lost and why that loss remains important. The critical issue arises when experiences situated within particular families or social environments become representative of Cuba as a whole.

The prosperity associated with this remembered Cuba had a historical basis. Robin D. Moore describes the country’s substantial affluence, professional class, and flourishing cultural industries alongside the inequalities and political violence of the period (26–31). Economic opportunity and an internationally influential cultural life coexisted with rural deprivation, racial discrimination, and repression under Batista. These conditions entered people’s lives unevenly. Memories centered on security, opportunity, or social standing can therefore be truthful accounts of particular experiences while leaving other experiences at the margins. A class perspective becomes especially consequential when one group’s access to prosperity is taken as a measure of national wellbeing.

Svetlana Boym’s distinction between restorative and reflective nostalgia offers a way to examine this movement from personal attachment to a general account of the past. Restorative nostalgia seeks to recover the lost home through claims of continuity and truth; reflective nostalgia leaves greater room for distance, ambiguity, and contradiction (chs. 4–5). These are tendencies within remembering, rather than fixed categories of people. Her distinction directs attention to how a cherished image of Cuba can become an authoritative version of its history, limiting the recognition of experiences that complicate it.

The documentary itself provides grounds for that complication. Olga’s earlier account associates the Revolution with opportunities unavailable to her before it, introducing a different relationship to the same historical transformation. Read together, these perspectives reveal how social position shapes what becomes memorable and what departure comes to mean. Recognizing the losses narrated by exiles can coexist with examining the limits of their account. The Cuba they remember belongs within the country’s history, alongside the lives and perspectives that their narrative does not fully contain.

Ana María and the Brigada Antonio Maceo: Reconnecting with Cuba

Ana María’s account of her participation in the Brigada Antonio Maceo introduces an organized effort to reconnect with Cuba into the documentary’s discussion of exile. Her involvement brings together questions explored in earlier fragments: the transmission of Cuban belonging, the interpretation of family memories, and the possibility of establishing a relationship with the island that differs from the positions inherited within a family.

The Brigade brought together young Cuban émigrés, many of whom had left the island as children following their parents’ decisions. A foundational visit in December 1977 took fifty-five young Cubans to Cuba for approximately three weeks, with authorization from the Cuban government. The program included family reunions, visits, and voluntary work. Named after the independence general Antonio Maceo, the organization defended the possibility of returning and developing renewed connections with the country (Torres 92–94).

These journeys also expressed a political position. Teishan A. Latner places the Brigade within the emergence of a Cuban American left influenced by the civil rights and anti–Vietnam War movements. Its participants sought reconciliation with the Cuban government and the normalization of relations between Cuba and the United States (Latner). Their engagement shows how political experiences acquired outside Cuba could encourage renewed involvement with the island. Maintaining Cuban identification could lead these young emigrants to question established positions within the exile community.

Reconnection nevertheless involved constraints and risks. Torres describes disagreements between later contingents and Cuban officials over ideological expectations and opportunities for contact with residents of the island (94). Supporters of dialogue also faced threats and violence abroad. In Puerto Rico, Brigade member Carlos Muñiz Varela, associated with the travel agency Viajes Varadero, was assassinated in 1979 (100–01). The history of these encounters therefore includes both the initiative of young emigrants and the political forces shaping the conditions under which they could act.

Read alongside Ana María’s earlier account of her parents’ decision to leave Cuba, her participation in the Brigade reveals how different relationships with the island could emerge within a family’s history. Levitt and Glick Schiller emphasize that generational experiences are shaped by socialization and relationships that can extend across borders (1017–18). This perspective helps us understand the significance of her participation: inherited attachments could acquire new meanings through political involvement and encounters with contemporary Cuba. The family’s departure remained part of that history, while a later generation developed its own ways of engaging with the country.

Returning to the Place Where Life Began

For some participants, returning to Cuba offers the possibility of seeing where they were born and placing that origin within the story of their lives. The visit brings a geographical reference into direct experience. For those who left young, the encounter may combine recognition with discovery: the place belongs to their biography, even when their memories of it are limited or intertwined with accounts received from others.

In *Impossible Returns: Narratives of the Cuban Diaspora*, Iraida H. López examines physical and imagined returns among Cubans who emigrated as children or adolescents. Her study considers both the emotional attachments and the tensions involved in their relationships with Cuba. This approach helps us distinguish between a birthplace as a physical location and the meanings it acquires through recollection, storytelling, and imagination. A visit brings these dimensions into contact, creating an opportunity to reconsider how the place fits within one’s understanding of self (López).

Research on temporary home visits offers a useful comparison. In a study of African migrants living in South Africa, Sabine Marschall finds that encounters with places, objects, and relationships associated with an autobiographical past can contribute to changes in how people understand themselves. Although her research concerns a different migration context, it directs attention to the significance of encountering a place in person after living elsewhere (Marschall).

Read through these perspectives, the value of returning can lie in the encounter itself. Questions about permanent residence remain separate from the wish to see one’s birthplace. The visit may establish connections, revise expectations, or reveal distance between a remembered place and its present circumstances. It also becomes a new experience that enters the person’s account of Cuba. Someone may understand their Cuban origins differently through that journey while continuing to locate home and everyday belonging in Puerto Rico.**Returning to the Place Where Life Began**

Exile and the Question of Community Continuity

Andrés Candelario describes a crisis of continuity within the Cuban exile community in Puerto Rico. In his account, subsequent immigration has not renewed the community on a scale comparable to the successive arrivals associated with Miami. His observation, situated within the documentary’s 2013 perspective, concerns the future of a community whose historical formation remains closely associated with the departures of earlier decades.

There is a historical basis for this contrast. In a later overview of Cuban and Dominican migration to Puerto Rico, Jorge Duany documents the rapid growth of Cuban immigration during the 1960s and its sharp decline beginning in the early 1980s. He notes that relatively few participants in the Mariel exodus settled in Puerto Rico, with limited immigration continuing afterward (“Inmigración”). This pattern helps contextualize Candelario’s concern without implying that Cuban migration to Puerto Rico ceased altogether.

Sociologist Tomás R. Jiménez uses the concept of immigrant replenishment to examine how continuing arrivals influence established communities and the identifications of their descendants. His research concerns Mexican Americans in the United States, where successive arrivals shape both relationships with other groups and expectations of cultural authenticity within the population of Mexican origin (1529–30). As a comparative framework, replenishment directs attention to the conditions under which a community sustains its connections to a country of origin through encounters between established residents and newcomers.

The documentary’s earlier discussions of children and grandchildren introduce a further dimension. Demographic renewal through immigration and the intergenerational transmission of an exile identity involve different processes. Descendants may sustain Cuban traditions, participate in institutions such as Casa Cuba, and preserve family memories while understanding Puerto Rico as home. Their participation provides forms of continuity that may differ from the experience and self-understanding of those who left Cuba.

New immigration would also bring change. Duany’s comparative research emphasizes that successive Cuban migration waves have differed in social composition and historical circumstances, and that Miami should not serve as the model for every Cuban settlement (“Cuban Communities” 70, 73). Newcomers cannot simply be expected to reproduce an earlier generation’s relationship with Cuba. Candelario’s concern therefore opens a discussion about what is understood to be at risk: the size of the migrant population, the continuity of its institutions, or the persistence of a particular way of defining exile. These questions are connected, but each requires its own evidence.

Political Change, Nonviolent Opposition, and the Exile Community

Guillermo Toledo brings two historical moments into conversation: the understanding between the United States and the Soviet Union that ended the 1962 missile crisis, and the development of peaceful opposition within Cuba. His remarks connect the international circumstances surrounding the revolutionary government with later efforts to pursue political change from within the island. He also identifies an acceptance of nonviolent methods among Cuban exiles in Puerto Rico.

The settlement reached by President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in October 1962 linked the withdrawal of Soviet missiles from Cuba with U.S. assurances against invasion. A separate, private understanding concerned the removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey (Office of the Historian). Read alongside the documentary’s accounts of an anticipated temporary exile, this settlement complicates expectations that U.S. military intervention would bring a rapid political reversal and make return possible. It did not, however, end the broader conflict: an April 1963 memorandum by U.S. official Sterling J. Cottrell documents continuing covert policy and proposals against the Cuban government.

Toledo’s discussion of peaceful opposition introduces another setting for political action. Public demonstrations, independent journalism, and human rights advocacy provide concrete examples of nonviolent activity documented before the film’s release. Amnesty International’s 2013 report, covering events in 2012, describes restrictions and detentions affecting people engaged in these activities, including members of the Damas de Blanco (Amnesty International). This record helps situate his observations within the documentary’s historical moment. Nonviolence concerns the methods through which demands are pursued; it does not establish that all opposition groups share the same political program.

His assessment of attitudes in Puerto Rico also adds to the documentary’s account of political differences within the diaspora. Bert Hoffmann argues that emigration can give rise to political voice exercised across borders, with consequences for the country of origin (26–27). Toledo’s remarks suggest a particular relationship between such engagement abroad and initiatives within Cuba: exiles can support methods pursued by people who remain on the island. His account thus presents political belonging as something expressed through judgments about how change should be sought and whose initiatives deserve support. The exile community’s relationship with Cuba includes responses to political developments occurring after its members’ departure.

Blame, Generations, and Political Responsibility

In this sequence of *Ecos del Exilio*, an argument over blame becomes a dispute about responsibility across generations. Some speakers hold those who supported Fidel Castro and subsequently emigrated responsible for Cuba’s political situation. Others point out that they had not yet been born, while references to imprisonment introduce the risks of challenging government authority. These responses bring different historical positions into conversation: those who participated in the revolutionary period, those who inherited its consequences, and those whose political choices were shaped by the threat of punishment.

References to having voted for Fidel require historical clarification when associated with the revolutionary transition of 1959. Castro did not enter office through a presidential election that year. His appointment as prime minister took place within the provisional revolutionary government, through cabinet arrangements documented in a contemporary diplomatic telegram (Braddock). Distinguishing popular support from an electoral mandate matters for the interpretation of responsibility. Supporting the struggle against Batista cannot, by itself, establish a person’s endorsement of every subsequent government policy. Such judgments require attention to particular actions, the information available at the time, and the authority individuals actually exercised.

In “Collective Responsibility,” Hannah Arendt distinguishes personal guilt from forms of responsibility that extend beyond an individual’s own actions. Guilt concerns participation in particular acts; people can nevertheless bear consequences and responsibilities arising from a political history they did not personally produce (43–44). Applied to the documentary, this distinction helps explain why the disagreement cannot be resolved simply by identifying who supported the Revolution. Younger generations encounter Cuba through circumstances and family narratives shaped by earlier decisions, but that inheritance does not establish their culpability. Their responses also raise the question of what obligations toward Cuba can arise from a history they did not initiate.

The invocation of imprisonment complicates judgments about what citizens should have done. Near the time of the documentary’s production, Amnesty International’s 2013 report, covering events in 2012, documented detentions and threats against people exercising freedoms of expression, association, and assembly (Amnesty International). This evidence provides a contemporary context for the fear mentioned in the fragment. It also underscores the need to examine the conditions under which political choices become possible or dangerous. Silence cannot be treated as sufficient evidence of agreement when expressing disagreement may carry substantial personal consequences.

The exchange reveals a tension between the collective consequences of Cuba’s political history and the unequal capacity of individuals to influence its course. Assigning blame to entire generations risks conflating distinct forms of participation and obscuring the accountability of those who exercised state power. Political judgment requires distinctions among governing, supporting a movement, accommodating authority, and opposing it under constraint. Within the diaspora portrayed in the documentary, these distinctions also shape expectations of later generations: how to remain politically engaged with Cuba without turning family history into an inherited debt.

Beyond Political Estrangement: Transnational Ties and Remittances

Ana María questions an image of Cuban exile defined by extremism and political intransigence. Her assessment of the difficulties of dialogue with the Cuban government appears alongside a discussion of connections sustained through research initiatives, civil society, and Catholic and Afro-Cuban religious networks. Situated in 2013, the fragment draws attention to relationships that a polarized representation of Cuba and its diaspora leaves insufficiently explained. Political antagonism coexists with exchanges through which Cubans on the island and abroad remain involved in one another’s lives.

The history of dialogue requires an important qualification. In November and December 1978, representatives of Cuban communities abroad met with the Cuban government in the negotiations known as *El Diálogo*. Their agenda included political prisoners, family reunification, and visits to relatives on the island (Torres 95). Ana María’s criticism can therefore be read as an assessment of the limits of political dialogue, rather than evidence that encounters had never occurred. The existence of negotiations and the possibility of sustaining relationships across political disagreement are related but distinct questions.

Religious networks give these connections a concrete social form. Research by Katrin Hansing and Sarah J. Mahler documents Catholic, Protestant, and Afro-Cuban ties linking Cuba and Miami before the documentary’s production. These relationships involved material assistance, communications, visits, and shared religious practices (124–26). Their participants pursued different objectives, ranging from reconciliation to political change (127). Religious affiliation thus created opportunities for contact without necessarily producing political agreement. The networks discussed in the fragment complicate the assumption that the exile community spoke with a single voice or maintained a uniform relationship with Cuba.

The economic crisis known as the Special Period gave assistance from abroad increasing importance. The collapse of the Soviet bloc and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 disrupted the trade and support on which Cuba’s economy had depended. Remittances—money migrants send to relatives or others in their country of origin—became an important means of financing household consumption. Susan Eckstein explains that the Cuban government also encouraged these transfers as a source of foreign currency, accessing part of their value through the state-controlled retail system (Eckstein). Money sent to sustain family life consequently entered an economic arrangement from which both recipients and the state could benefit, although their interests did not always coincide.

Within the documentary’s 2013 perspective, continuing economic hardship makes these exchanges central to understanding the relationship between migration and everyday life. A person represented in political discourse as an adversary could also be a relative whose contributions helped sustain a household. Sending money did not, by itself, establish support for the Cuban government; opposition to that government did not necessarily dissolve family obligations. The attention to Cuba–Miami connections also places the documentary’s Puerto Rican setting within a wider diasporic field. Exile emerges here as a relationship continually reshaped by political disagreement, religious affiliation, and the material responsibilities that cross national borders.

Family Memory and the Authority to Interpret Cuba

Near the end of *Ecos del Exilio*, the juxtaposition of interviews with descendants brings disagreement over visiting Cuba into focus. Several speakers advocate a change in attitude and challenge the position that they should not travel to the island. Others reaffirm established exile perspectives, express curiosity, or describe fears shaped by relatives’ accounts. The montage places these responses in conversation, revealing differences both across generations and among descendants themselves. Generational succession emerges as a process whose political meaning remains unsettled.

These disagreements concern the authority of family memory over present decisions. As Robyn Fivush argues, remembering involves interpretations that are shared, negotiated, and contested through social interaction (46). In this sequence, accounts of Cuba provide descendants with explanations of their family’s departure and frameworks for evaluating future contact with the island. An account of past danger can become a prescription for present conduct. The point of contention is therefore how far recognition of a relative’s experience should entail accepting the choices that the relative considers appropriate.

The expressions of fear make the emotional weight of this relationship particularly visible. Accounts received through trusted relatives can shape expectations of Cuba before a possible visit, giving earlier experiences a continuing presence in decisions about travel. Curiosity introduces the possibility of placing received knowledge in dialogue with another experience. Questioning the injunction against visiting can thus be read as a claim to interpretive authority: an assertion that descendants should participate in deciding how Cuba will figure in their own lives. Such a position need not dismiss family suffering or imply agreement with the Cuban government. It makes the relationship between remembrance, loyalty, and personal judgment open to reconsideration.

The coexistence of these positions complicates a linear account in which younger generations inevitably abandon exile politics or move toward reconciliation. Levitt and Glick Schiller’s critique of linear generational models helps situate these differences within relationships and forms of socialization that cross national boundaries (1017–18). Descendants can sustain, revise, or question inherited positions while remaining engaged with the histories through which those positions acquired meaning. At this stage of the documentary, the future of exile memory becomes a question of how that inheritance will be interpreted and acted upon. Its transmission includes disagreement over which lessons the past authorizes and who has the authority to draw them.

Longing for Return and the Limits of Recognition

Jay Martínez expresses his longing to return to Cuba while describing the difficulty of being recognized as belonging in either Cuba or Puerto Rico. He believes that others will never consider him Puerto Rican, yet he also describes being regarded as a foreigner by Cubans living on the island. His account brings the desire for return into tension with the possibility that neither place will recognize him on the terms he seeks.

Marco Antonsich’s distinction between personal feelings of belonging and the politics of belonging helps clarify this tension. The former concerns the intimate experience of feeling at home; the latter concerns the practices and judgments through which membership is claimed, granted, or contested (Antonsich). Martínez’s remarks make the relationship between these dimensions particularly visible. Attachment to Cuba persists alongside the perception that people living there regard him as an outsider. The longing for a place does not give an individual exclusive authority to determine how that connection will be received.

Return consequently acquires a meaning that geographical movement alone cannot resolve. In Martínez’s account, Cuba remains a desired destination, but recognition as Cuban is uncertain. Being considered foreign suggests that leaving the island can become a basis for questioning an emigrant’s membership in its national community. His remarks identify a painful asymmetry: the place to which someone wishes to return can remain central to that person’s life while its residents understand the relationship differently. The foreignness he describes concerns social recognition; it does not, by itself, establish his legal nationality.

Near the documentary’s conclusion, this account complicates earlier expressions of coexisting Cuban and Puerto Rican identifications. Multiple affiliations can be meaningful to individuals while remaining contested by others. The phrase *ni de aquí ni de allá* acquires a relational significance here: it names the difficulty of securing recognition across places with which a person maintains a connection. Martínez’s longing does not resolve that difficulty. It leaves return invested with hope while exposing the uncertainty of what returning could restore.
